1	\section{Discussion}

4	The oracle experiments (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}, bottom) constitute causal interventions that isolate the source of failure. By replacing only the constraint source while holding all other pipeline components fixed, we establish that aggregation is not the bottleneck: the $+8.82$\,pp improvement on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$) pinpoint same-model self-extraction as the single point of failure. This oracle design follows established methodology where component-level interventions isolate error sources \citep{press2023compositionality, trivedi2023ircot, saparov2023greedy}.
5	
6	Constraint quality analysis on the full Qwen2.5-14B dataset (804 problems, 307 with multiple candidates, 7{,}844 unique constraints) explains the mechanism through two complementary metrics. \emph{Source-trace discriminativeness} measures whether a constraint's weight is concentrated on traces producing a single answer: 39.2\% of constraint weight is source-discriminative (95\% CI [38.7, 39.8]). \emph{Z3 semantic discriminativeness} asks whether a constraint can evaluate differently across candidates under Z3: only 8.2\% of constraints are semantically discriminative (95\% CI [7.6, 8.8]). The gap between these rates reveals the mechanism: constraints are statistically correlated with their source answers (39.2\%) but semantically equivalent across all candidates (91.8\%). Domain constraints encode shared facts (predicate definitions, background implications, intermediate steps) that Z3 satisfies identically regardless of the answer; only answer-assertion constraints carry semantic discriminative power. This structural analysis confirms that switching the scoring mechanism from source-trace attribution to direct Z3 evaluation would not change the outcome. The 803/804 agreement between MAX-SAT and count-only (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) provides independent empirical confirmation.
7	
8	The computational cost is substantial: constraint extraction accounts for 48.7\% of total SICA pipeline time (measured on Qwen2.5-14B, FOLIO + ProofWriter combined, $n = 804$, single A6000 GPU), roughly doubling wall-clock cost compared to SC alone. SICA and SC disagree on 31 of 804 problems (3.9\%), but these disagreements approximately cancel: 16 SICA wins, 14 SC wins, and 1 both-wrong with different answers, yielding a net gain of only $+$2 problems (Appendix~\ref{app:case-studies} provides representative case studies). Bootstrap confidence intervals bound the true effect to [$-1.12$, $+1.62$]\,pp for the largest confirmatory condition ($n = 804$; Appendix Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap}): even if a small effect exists, it cannot justify the pipeline's additional complexity and cost.
9	
10	The oracle ceilings ($+8.82$\,pp on FOLIO, $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter) quantify the potential locked behind the capability trap, with larger gains on harder relational reasoning subtypes (RelNeg $+17.86$\,pp). The oracle gap suggests that constraint quality, not the extraction prompt format, is the primary bottleneck, though alternative extraction strategies (e.g., few-shot examples, iterative refinement, structured decomposition) were not tested in this study. Three concrete paths can unlock the potential. First, trained FOL extractors supervised on datasets with gold annotations (such as FOLIO) can learn extraction patterns that exceed same-model capabilities; FoVer \citep{wang2025fover} demonstrates this approach with a dedicated verifier. Second, external provers that verify constraints independently of the reasoning model eliminate the circular dependency between generation and verification. Third, cross-model extraction, where a separate model extracts constraints from another model's traces, breaks the self-reference loop that produces non-discriminative constraints. Each path targets the extraction bottleneck directly; since MAX-SAT and count-only produce identical predictions on 803/804 instances, improving the aggregation mechanism offers no path forward.
11	
12	For practitioners considering constraint-based voting, $C_0$ provides a zero-cost screening criterion computable from the trace sampling stage alone, before any constraint extraction or solver invocation. When $C_0$ falls below 5\%, SICA degenerates to SC by construction. High $C_0$ is necessary but not sufficient, as the capability trap renders constraints non-discriminative even when disagreement is abundant ($C_0 = 61.8\%$, $\Delta = -2.45$~pp, n.s., for LLaMA-3.1-8B on FOLIO). The recommended workflow is: compute $C_0$, and if it exceeds 5\%, assess constraint quality on a small pilot before committing to full-scale extraction. More broadly, the evaluation framework developed here (oracle component isolation, dual discriminativeness metrics, and $C_0$ screening) applies to any pipeline where an LLM extracts formal structure from its own outputs. This reusable methodology can diagnose self-extraction bottlenecks beyond the SICA setting.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The oracle experiments (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}, bottom) constitute causal interventions that isolate the source of failure. By replacing only the constraint source while holding all other pipeline components fixed, we establish that aggregation is not the bottleneck: the $+8.82$\,pp improvement on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$) pinpoint same-model self-extraction as the single point of failure. This oracle design follows established methodology where component-level interventions isolate error sources \citep{press2023compositionality, trivedi2023ircot, saparov2023greedy}.

Constraint quality analysis on the full Qwen2.5-14B dataset (804 problems, 307 with multiple candidates, 7{,}844 unique constraints) explains the mechanism through two complementary metrics. \emph{Source-trace discriminativeness} measures whether a constraint's weight is concentrated on traces producing a single answer: 39.2\% of constraint weight is source-discriminative (95\% CI [38.7, 39.8]). \emph{Z3 semantic discriminativeness} asks whether a constraint can evaluate differently across candidates under Z3: only 8.2\% of constraints are semantically discriminative (95\% CI [7.6, 8.8]). The gap between these rates reveals the mechanism: constraints are statistically correlated with their source answers (39.2\%) but semantically equivalent across all candidates (91.8\%). Domain constraints encode shared facts (predicate definitions, background implications, intermediate steps) that Z3 satisfies identically regardless of the answer; only answer-assertion constraints carry semantic discriminative power. This structural analysis confirms that switching the scoring mechanism from source-trace attribution to direct Z3 evaluation would not change the outcome. The 803/804 agreement between MAX-SAT and count-only (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) provides independent empirical confirmation.

The computational cost is substantial: constraint extraction accounts for 48.7\% of total SICA pipeline time (measured on Qwen2.5-14B, FOLIO + ProofWriter combined, $n = 804$, single A6000 GPU), roughly doubling wall-clock cost compared to SC alone. SICA and SC disagree on 31 of 804 problems (3.9\%), but these disagreements approximately cancel: 16 SICA wins, 14 SC wins, and 1 both-wrong with different answers, yielding a net gain of only $+$2 problems (Appendix~\ref{app:case-studies} provides representative case studies). Bootstrap confidence intervals bound the true effect to [$-1.12$, $+1.62$]\,pp for the largest confirmatory condition ($n = 804$; Appendix Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap}): even if a small effect exists, it cannot justify the pipeline's additional complexity and cost.

The oracle ceilings ($+8.82$\,pp on FOLIO, $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter) quantify the potential locked behind the capability trap, with larger gains on harder relational reasoning subtypes (RelNeg $+17.86$\,pp). The oracle gap suggests that constraint quality, not the extraction prompt format, is the primary bottleneck, though alternative extraction strategies (e.g., few-shot examples, iterative refinement, structured decomposition) were not tested in this study. Three concrete paths can unlock the potential. First, trained FOL extractors supervised on datasets with gold annotations (such as FOLIO) can learn extraction patterns that exceed same-model capabilities; FoVer \citep{wang2025fover} demonstrates this approach with a dedicated verifier. Second, external provers that verify constraints independently of the reasoning model eliminate the circular dependency between generation and verification. Third, cross-model extraction, where a separate model extracts constraints from another model's traces, breaks the self-reference loop that produces non-discriminative constraints. Each path targets the extraction bottleneck directly; since MAX-SAT and count-only produce identical predictions on 803/804 instances, improving the aggregation mechanism offers no path forward.

For practitioners considering constraint-based voting, $C_0$ provides a zero-cost screening criterion computable from the trace sampling stage alone, before any constraint extraction or solver invocation. When $C_0$ falls below 5\%, SICA degenerates to SC by construction. High $C_0$ is necessary but not sufficient, as the capability trap renders constraints non-discriminative even when disagreement is abundant ($C_0 = 61.8\%$, $\Delta = -2.45$~pp, n.s., for LLaMA-3.1-8B on FOLIO). The recommended workflow is: compute $C_0$, and if it exceeds 5\%, assess constraint quality on a small pilot before committing to full-scale extraction. More broadly, the evaluation framework developed here (oracle component isolation, dual discriminativeness metrics, and $C_0$ screening) applies to any pipeline where an LLM extracts formal structure from its own outputs. This reusable methodology can diagnose self-extraction bottlenecks beyond the SICA setting.

       ```latex
       \subsection{Z3 Feedback Refinement}
       \label{sec:z3-feedback}
       
       The standard SICA pipeline extracts constraints in a single open-loop pass, with no feedback from the solver to the extraction model. Z3 Feedback Refinement introduces a closed loop between the solver and the LLM, an instance of the LLM-Modulo paradigm \citep{kambhampati2024position} where an external verifier provides signals that the model cannot generate through introspection alone.
       
       After initial constraint extraction (\S\ref{sec:constraint-extraction}), Z3 performs a consistency check on each trace's constraint set. When Z3 identifies an unsatisfiable subset, it returns the minimal UNSAT core: the smallest set of mutually contradictory constraints. A refinement prompt presents the UNSAT core alongside the original reasoning trace and asks the LLM to resolve the contradiction by revising or replacing the conflicting constraints. The refined constraints replace the originals, and the consistency check repeats for up to $N = 3$ rounds or until the constraint set is satisfiable. The final refined constraints enter the standard MAX-SAT scoring pipeline (\S\ref{sec:maxsat}).
       
       The key distinction from standard self-extraction is the source of the corrective signal. In standard SICA, the LLM extracts constraints without any feedback on their logical coherence. In Z3 Feedback Refinement, the solver identifies specific contradictions that the LLM missed, providing an external verification signal. Whether this signal is sufficient to improve constraint discriminativeness is an empirical question (\S\ref{sec:diagnostics}).
       ```

file.content: Several limitations bound the scope of our conclusions. First, the oracle experiments cover two formal logic benchmarks (FOLIO $n = 204$, ProofWriter $n = 600$) that provide gold annotations; extending this analysis to commonsense or science domains requires constructing comparable gold constraint sets for those domains. Second, seven of our eleven model-domain conditions have $n \leq 60$, providing insufficient statistical power for confirmatory claims; power analysis shows that the minimum detectable effect exceeds 5\,pp for these conditions (Appendix Table~\ref{tab:power}), so they serve as regime characterization rather than definitive tests. Third, we do not compare against trained FOL extractors or cross-model extraction pipelines; our findings characterize the limitations of same-model self-extraction specifically. Fourth, all models tested range from 7B to 32B parameters; whether the capability trap persists at larger scales (70B+) remains an open question. Fifth, our extraction prompts use a single zero-shot template per domain; alternative prompting strategies (few-shot exemplars, chain-of-thought extraction, or iterative refinement) might yield higher-quality constraints, though the oracle gap suggests the bottleneck is fundamental rather than prompt-specific. Sixth, the constraint quality analysis (8.2\% Z3 semantic discriminative rate, 39.2\% source-trace discriminative rate) covers Qwen2.5-14B on the full FOLIO + ProofWriter dataset ($N = 804$); other model-domain combinations may exhibit different constraint characteristics. Seventh, constraint extraction uses $T_{\text{ext}} = 0.3$ while trace sampling uses $T = 0.7$; alternative extraction temperatures might yield different constraint characteristics, though our negative results suggest the bottleneck is semantic coupling rather than extraction diversity. Eighth, StrategyQA and ARC-Challenge use the mathematical extraction prompt rather than the logical one because their reasoning structure does not involve formal predicates or implications (Appendix~\ref{app:prompts}); a domain-specific commonsense extraction template might yield different constraint characteristics for these benchmarks. Ninth, although we prompt for FOL-style formalizations, the extracted constraints are predominantly propositional ground clauses without quantifiers (\S\ref{sec:constraint-extraction}); whether models capable of producing genuine quantified FOL would yield higher discriminative rates is untested. Tenth, deduplication uses syntactic equivalence, so semantically equivalent constraints with different surface forms receive separate weights, potentially inflating the apparent constraint pool without adding discriminative content. Eleventh, the GSM8K pilot ($n = 30$) is included to illustrate the constraint-absent failure regime and should not be interpreted as confirmatory evidence.

# Paper Framing Upgrade — Two Frameworks for EMNLP 2026 ARR May 25

Prepared: 2026-05-18. Based on current paper state + 3 new extraction methods in progress.

---

## Framework A: "Diagnosis + Method" (at least one method works)

### Trigger Condition
disc_rate improves from ~8% to 20%+ AND accuracy gain >= +2pp (significant or near-significant) for at least one of: Contrastive Extraction, Z3 Feedback Refinement, Cross-Model Extraction.

### Title Options
1. "Breaking the Capability Trap: Contrastive Constraint Extraction for LLM Self-Verification"
2. "From Diagnosis to Remedy: Overcoming Non-Discriminative Constraints in LLM Self-Verification"
3. "Discriminative by Design: Targeted Extraction Methods for Symbolic LLM Consensus"

### Abstract Framework (~220 words)
1. **Problem** (2 sent): Neuro-symbolic methods extract FOL constraints from LLM reasoning traces for answer aggregation, but whether self-extraction produces useful constraints has not been evaluated. If it works, no trained verifier or external prover is needed.
2. **Gap** (1 sent): We show standard self-extraction falls into a capability trap: constraints are semantically coupled to source answers and carry no discriminative signal (only [X]% evaluate differently across candidates).
3. **Method** (2-3 sent): We diagnose the trap across [N] models and [N] domains, then design three targeted interventions: contrastive extraction (forcing answer-discriminative constraints), Z3 feedback refinement (iterative solver-guided re-extraction), and cross-model extraction (breaking self-reference). [BEST_METHOD] achieves [PLACEHOLDER_DISC_RATE]% discriminative rate (vs. [BASELINE]% baseline).
4. **Result** (2 sent): [BEST_METHOD]-SICA improves over SC by +[PLACEHOLDER]pp on [DATASET] (p=[PLACEHOLDER]). The oracle ceiling (+8.82pp) remains partially unreached, but [BEST_METHOD] recovers [X]% of the gap, demonstrating that targeted extraction design can partially break the capability trap.

### Introduction Narrative (5 paragraphs)

**P1 — Background**: Neuro-symbolic methods (Logic-LM, LINC, DyLoS, Aristotle, FoVer) augment LLM reasoning with symbolic solvers and report gains on logical benchmarks. A critical commonality: all introduce capabilities beyond the reasoning model itself. Self-extraction would provide a lightweight, portable alternative.

**P2 — Problem importance**: Self-Consistency remains the dominant aggregation method but treats traces as black boxes, discarding intermediate reasoning structure. SC's known scaling plateau (Loo et al. 2025) motivates methods that extract richer signal. Yet no work has systematically evaluated whether self-extraction produces useful constraints.

**P3 — Capability trap diagnosis**: We evaluate SICA (MAX-SAT over self-extracted FOL) across six models, three domains, N>1,300 instances. Result: zero significant improvement. Manual analysis reveals only [X]% of constraints discriminate between candidates. Oracle control (+8.82pp, p<0.001) confirms the aggregation mechanism works; the bottleneck is extraction quality. We term this the capability trap.

**P4 — Our interventions**: The trap has a specific mechanism: constraints mirror their source answers because the same model generates both. We design three interventions targeting this mechanism: (1) contrastive extraction forces the model to generate constraints that distinguish between competing answers, (2) Z3 feedback refinement uses solver results to iteratively improve constraint quality, (3) cross-model extraction breaks self-reference by using a different model. [BEST_METHOD] raises discriminative rate from [X]% to [Y]% and yields +[Z]pp accuracy gain.

**P5 — Contributions**:
- C1: Characterize the capability trap in same-model constraint extraction (six models, three domains, N>1,300)
- C2: Design three targeted interventions grounded in the diagnosed failure mechanism
- C3: Show [BEST_METHOD] partially breaks the trap: disc_rate [X]->[Y]%, accuracy +[Z]pp, recovering [W]% of the oracle ceiling
- C4: Provide C0 diagnostic and practical guidelines for when symbolic aggregation is worth pursuing

### Method Section Additions

Current S3 (SICA Pipeline) stays as-is. Add:

**S3.5 Contrastive Extraction**
- Input: K traces with candidate answers, the set of distinct answers A(q)
- Key change: extraction prompt includes ALL candidate answers and explicitly asks "what constraint would distinguish answer X from answer Y?"
- Template structure: "The following traces disagree on the answer. Traces 1,3,5 say True. Traces 2,4,6 say False. Extract a FOL constraint that evaluates differently for True vs False."
- Rationale: forces the model to attend to inter-answer differences rather than intra-trace facts
- Cost: same number of LLM calls (one per trace), but prompt is longer (includes answer distribution)

**S3.6 Z3 Feedback Refinement**
- Iterative loop: extract -> Z3 evaluate against all candidates -> identify non-discriminative constraints -> feedback to model -> re-extract
- Feedback prompt: "The following constraints you extracted evaluate identically for all candidate answers: [list]. These are not useful. Extract constraints that evaluate differently for True vs False."
- Max iterations: 3 (diminishing returns expected)
- Inspired by Logic-LM's self-refinement but applied to constraint quality rather than parse correctness
- Cost: up to 3x extraction calls per trace

**S3.7 Cross-Model Extraction**
- Model A generates traces, Model B extracts constraints from Model A's traces
- Breaks the self-reference: Model B's extraction biases are independent of Model A's generation biases
- Tested pairs: Mistral-7B extracts from Qwen-14B traces, Qwen-14B extracts from LLaMA-8B traces
- Cost: same as baseline (one extraction call per trace), but requires two models

### Results Section Additions

**New Table 5: Extraction Method Comparison**
| Method | disc_rate (%) | Acc (%) | Delta vs SC (pp) | Delta vs baseline SICA (pp) |
|--------|-------------|---------|------------------|---------------------------|
| SC (majority vote) | --- | [X] | --- | --- |
| SICA (baseline) | [X] | [X] | [X] | --- |
| SICA + Contrastive | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] |
| SICA + Z3 Refinement | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] |
| SICA + Cross-Model | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] |
| Oracle (gold FOL) | ~100 | 88.24 | +8.82 | +8.82 |

Primary: Qwen2.5-14B on FOLIO (n=204) + ProofWriter (n=600).

**New Table 6: Qwen3-14B Generational Comparison**
| Model | Mode | SC (%) | SICA (%) | disc_rate (%) | Delta (pp) |
|-------|------|--------|----------|--------------|--------|
| Qwen2.5-14B | standard | [X] | [X] | [X] | [X] |
| Qwen3-14B | non-thinking | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] |
| Qwen3-14B | thinking | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] | [PLACEHOLDER] |

**New Figure: disc_rate vs Accuracy Improvement**
- Scatter: x = disc_rate (%), y = Delta(SICA-SC) in pp
- Points: all conditions (baseline + 3 methods x datasets)
- Narrative intent: "disc_rate is the binding bottleneck; improving it translates to accuracy gains"

### Discussion Key Paragraphs (Framework A)

1. **Why [BEST_METHOD] works**: Mechanism explanation connecting back to capability trap diagnosis.
2. **Remaining gap to oracle**: Even best method recovers only [W]% of +8.82pp. What the gap represents.
3. **Cost-benefit**: [BEST_METHOD] overhead vs accuracy gain. Compare to SC baseline cost.
4. **Updated practical recommendation**: C0 -> if high, try [BEST_METHOD] -> pilot disc_rate check -> deploy.

---

## Framework B: "Systematic Diagnosis + Strong Negative" (all methods fail)

### Trigger Condition
All three methods produce disc_rate < 15% OR accuracy gain < +1.5pp (n.s.) across all tested conditions.

### Title Options
1. "The Capability Trap: Why LLMs Cannot Verify Their Own Reasoning Through Self-Extracted Constraints"
2. "Beyond Prompt Engineering: The Fundamental Limits of Self-Extracted Constraint Verification in LLMs"
3. "Three Roads to Nowhere: Systematic Evidence That Self-Extraction Cannot Break the Capability Trap"

### Abstract Framework (~220 words)
1. **Problem** (2 sent): Same as Framework A.
2. **Gap** (1 sent): Same capability trap diagnosis.
3. **Method** (2-3 sent): We diagnose the trap, then test three targeted interventions designed to break it: contrastive extraction, Z3 feedback refinement, and cross-model extraction. Each targets a specific hypothesized cause.
4. **Result** (2-3 sent): None of the three interventions significantly improves discriminative rate or accuracy. This rules out prompt-engineering explanations and establishes the capability trap as a fundamental limitation. The +8.82pp oracle ceiling remains achievable only with external formal knowledge.

### Introduction Narrative (5 paragraphs)

**P1-P3**: Same as Framework A (background, SC limitations, capability trap diagnosis).

**P4 — Systematic interventions**: The capability trap could stem from (a) prompt design (fixable with contrastive prompts), (b) solver feedback blindness (fixable with iterative refinement), or (c) self-reference circularity (fixable with cross-model). We test one intervention per hypothesis. If any succeeds, the trap is contingent; if all fail, it is fundamental to current LLM capabilities.

**P5 — Contributions**:
- C1: Characterize the capability trap across six models, three domains, N>1,300 instances
- C2: Test three targeted interventions, each addressing a specific hypothesized cause; all three fail
- C3: Rule out prompt-engineering and provide causal evidence (oracle +8.82pp) that external formal knowledge is required
- C4: C0 as zero-cost diagnostic; establish that trained verifiers are necessary for symbolic LLM verification

### Results Section Additions (Framework B)

Same table structure as Framework A, but narrative shifts:

"Despite targeting three distinct hypothesized causes, none of the interventions raise disc_rate above [X]% or achieve significant accuracy gain. The oracle ceiling (+8.82pp) remains exclusively accessible through external formal knowledge."

**Additional analysis unique to Framework B**:
- Per-intervention failure analysis: WHY each fails
  - Contrastive: model still generates constraints consistent with its own answer bias even when explicitly asked to discriminate
  - Refinement: re-extraction produces different but equally non-discriminative constraints (constraints are correct but vacuous)
  - Cross-model: Model B's extraction inherits Model A's trace structure, not truly independent
- Table: disc_rate per refinement iteration (showing plateau)

### Discussion Key Paragraphs (Framework B)

1. **Why all three fail**: Each intervention targets a surface symptom, not the root cause. Traces encode conclusions before justifications; extraction from conclusion-laden traces inevitably produces conclusion-coupled constraints.
2. **Implications**: Self-extraction pipelines cannot improve over SC without external knowledge. Trained extractors (FoVer), external provers (Logic-LM, LINC), and multi-paradigm solvers (DyLoS) succeed because they introduce knowledge the model lacks.
3. **What "fundamental" means**: Not that symbolic reasoning is useless, but that the formal knowledge must originate outside the reasoning model's own traces.
4. **Practical recommendation**: C0 screening stands, but stronger: if C0 > threshold, invest in trained extractors, not prompt engineering.

---

## Shared Elements (Both Frameworks)

### Current Structure Reuse (~80%)
- S1 Introduction: P1-P3 reusable, P4-P5 rewritten
- S2 Related Work: current text reusable, add 3-5 new citations
- S3 Method: S3.1-3.4 unchanged, add S3.5-3.7
- S4 Experiments: S4.1-4.4 unchanged, add S4.5 (new methods) + S4.6 (Qwen3)
- S5 Discussion: partially rewritten depending on framework
- S6 Conclusion: rewritten
- Abstract: rewritten

### Page Budget (8pp main limit)
Current: 8pp main. Adding 3 methods + new results + discussion = ~1.5pp extra.
Must cut ~1.5pp:
- Move temperature ablation detail to appendix (saves ~0.3pp)
- Compress ablation S4.4 table + text (saves ~0.2pp)
- Tighten Related Work (saves ~0.3pp)
- Move degeneration proof S3.4 to appendix (saves ~0.3pp)
- Merge current discussion into expanded discussion (saves ~0.3pp)

### Related Work Additions Needed (Both Frameworks)
- **Contrastive methods**: Contrastive Decoding (Li et al. 2023)
- **Self-refinement**: Self-Refine (Madaan et al. 2023), Logic-LM refinement (already cited)
- **Cross-model verification**: LLM-as-Judge, cross-model debate literature
- **CISC**: already cited (taubenfeld2025cisc)
- **RASC**: already cited (wan2024rasc)
- All new citations need verify_references before inclusion

---

## Experiment Suggestions and Insights

1. **Lead with disc_rate, not accuracy**: disc_rate is the mechanism-level metric. Accuracy is downstream consequence. Both needed, but disc_rate tells you whether the intervention is working at the right level.

2. **Contrastive prompt design is critical**: Must include actual answer distribution AND explicitly request distinguishing constraints. Test 2-3 prompt variants. A weak contrastive prompt ("extract important constraints") will fail just like baseline.

3. **Z3 Refinement: track disc_rate per iteration**: If disc_rate plateaus after round 1, further rounds are wasteful. This data is informative regardless of which framework we use.

4. **Cross-model: test BOTH directions**: Mistral->Qwen AND Qwen->Mistral. If direction matters (stronger extracting from weaker vs. vice versa), that reveals whether the issue is extraction capability or trace structure.

5. **Qwen3 thinking mode**: Most exciting condition. Extended internal CoT may produce qualitatively different traces. Measure trace length distribution alongside disc_rate. If thinking mode traces have more explicit intermediate steps, extraction might capture genuinely different constraints.

6. **Statistical power**: Run new methods on FOLIO (n=204) + ProofWriter (n=600) minimum. Combined n=804 gives MDE ~1.9pp. Running only n=204 gives MDE ~4.8pp, which may miss moderate effects.

7. **Cost tracking**: Record wall-clock time and token usage for each method. Framework A needs cost-benefit; Framework B needs "expensive interventions still fail."

8. **Define recovery metric**: recovery_rate = Delta_method / Delta_oracle x 100%. E.g., +2pp method / +8.82pp oracle = 22.7% recovery. Clean communication of progress toward ceiling.

9. **Contrastive may help Framework B too**: Even if contrastive extraction fails on accuracy, if it raises disc_rate from 8% to 15% but accuracy stays flat, that's evidence that higher disc_rate alone is insufficient (constraints are discriminative but wrong). This would strengthen the "fundamental" narrative.

10. **Cross-model with Qwen3**: If Qwen3 (thinking mode) extracts from Qwen2.5 traces, we get the strongest cross-model condition: generationally different model with extended reasoning capabilities doing extraction. Worth prioritizing.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The oracle experiments (Table~\ref{tab:main_results}, bottom) constitute causal interventions that isolate the source of failure. By replacing only the constraint source while holding all other pipeline components fixed, we establish that aggregation is not the bottleneck: the $+8.82$\,pp improvement on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$) pinpoint same-model self-extraction as the single point of failure. This oracle design follows established methodology where component-level interventions isolate error sources \citep{press2023compositionality, trivedi2023ircot, saparov2023greedy}.

Constraint quality analysis on the full Qwen2.5-14B dataset (804 problems, 307 with multiple candidates, 7{,}844 unique constraints) explains the mechanism through two complementary metrics. \emph{Source-trace discriminativeness} measures whether a constraint's weight is concentrated on traces producing a single answer: 39.2\% of constraint weight is source-discriminative (95\% CI [38.7, 39.8]). \emph{Z3 semantic discriminativeness} asks whether a constraint can evaluate differently across candidates under Z3: only 8.2\% of constraints are semantically discriminative (95\% CI [7.6, 8.8]). The gap between these rates reveals the mechanism: constraints are statistically correlated with their source answers (39.2\%) but semantically equivalent across all candidates (91.8\%). Domain constraints encode shared facts (predicate definitions, background implications, intermediate steps) that Z3 satisfies identically regardless of the answer; only answer-assertion constraints carry semantic discriminative power. This structural analysis confirms that switching the scoring mechanism from source-trace attribution to direct Z3 evaluation would not change the outcome. The 803/804 agreement between MAX-SAT and count-only (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}) provides independent empirical confirmation.

The computational cost is substantial: constraint extraction accounts for 48.7\% of total SICA pipeline time (measured on Qwen2.5-14B, FOLIO + ProofWriter combined, $n = 804$, single A6000 GPU), roughly doubling wall-clock cost compared to SC alone. SICA and SC disagree on 31 of 804 problems (3.9\%), but these disagreements approximately cancel: 16 SICA wins, 14 SC wins, and 1 both-wrong with different answers, yielding a net gain of only $+$2 problems (Appendix~\ref{app:case-studies} provides representative case studies). Bootstrap confidence intervals bound the true effect to [$-1.12$, $+1.62$]\,pp for the largest confirmatory condition ($n = 804$; Appendix Table~\ref{tab:bootstrap}): even if a small effect exists, it cannot justify the pipeline's additional complexity and cost.

The oracle ceilings ($+8.82$\,pp on FOLIO, $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter) quantify the potential locked behind the capability trap, with larger gains on harder relational reasoning subtypes (RelNeg $+17.86$\,pp). The oracle gap suggests that constraint quality, not the extraction prompt format, is the primary bottleneck, though alternative extraction strategies (e.g., few-shot examples, iterative refinement, structured decomposition) were not tested in this study. Three concrete paths can unlock the potential. First, trained FOL extractors supervised on datasets with gold annotations (such as FOLIO) can learn extraction patterns that exceed same-model capabilities; FoVer \citep{wang2025fover} demonstrates this approach with a dedicated verifier. Second, external provers that verify constraints independently of the reasoning model eliminate the circular dependency between generation and verification. Third, cross-model extraction, where a separate model extracts constraints from another model's traces, breaks the self-reference loop that produces non-discriminative constraints. Each path targets the extraction bottleneck directly; since MAX-SAT and count-only produce identical predictions on 803/804 instances, improving the aggregation mechanism offers no path forward.

For practitioners considering constraint-based voting, $C_0$ provides a zero-cost screening criterion computable from the trace sampling stage alone, before any constraint extraction or solver invocation. When $C_0$ falls below 5\%, SICA degenerates to SC by construction. High $C_0$ is necessary but not sufficient, as the capability trap renders constraints non-discriminative even when disagreement is abundant ($C_0 = 61.8\%$, $\Delta = -2.45$~pp, n.s., for LLaMA-3.1-8B on FOLIO). The recommended workflow is: compute $C_0$, and if it exceeds 5\%, assess constraint quality on a small pilot before committing to full-scale extraction. More broadly, the evaluation framework developed here (oracle component isolation, dual discriminativeness metrics, and $C_0$ screening) applies to any pipeline where an LLM extracts formal structure from its own outputs. This reusable methodology can diagnose self-extraction bottlenecks beyond the SICA setting.

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluated Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation across six models spanning three base architectures (Qwen, Mistral, LLaMA) from 7B to 32B parameters, including instruction-tuned, reasoning-specialized, and distilled variants, and three reasoning domains with more than 1,500 total instances. Self-extracted SICA provides no statistically significant improvement over Self-Consistency in any tested condition, with accuracy gaps ranging from $-3.3$ to $+3.3$\,pp. Oracle experiments replacing self-extraction with gold annotations yield $+8.82$\,pp on FOLIO and $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter (both $p < 0.001$). This result causally localizes the failure to extraction quality: the MAX-SAT aggregation mechanism is sound when supplied with high-quality constraints, but same-model self-extraction cannot produce them. We characterize this as a \emph{capability trap}: because the reasoning model also extracts the constraints, those constraints inherit the same biases that produced potentially flawed answers and carry no independent discriminative signal. The failure is not one of aggregation design but of the circular dependency between generation and verification within a single model.

The practical consequences follow from the constraint quality analysis (\S\ref{sec:diagnostics}, \S\ref{sec:ablation}). Over 91\% of self-extracted constraints are semantically non-discriminative (8.2\% Z3 semantic discriminative rate, $N = 804$), which reduces MAX-SAT to a weighted vote count (803/804 agreement with count-only). The extraction step roughly doubles wall-clock cost for zero expected gain. For practitioners, the multi-candidate rate $C_0$ provides a zero-cost screening criterion computable from trace samples alone: low $C_0$ rules out any SICA benefit by construction, while high $C_0$ warrants a constraint quality audit before committing to full-scale extraction.

The oracle gaps ($+8.82$\,pp on FOLIO, $+11.50$\,pp on ProofWriter, combined $N = 804$) quantify recoverable potential in formal logic domains; extension to commonsense and science domains requires constructing comparable gold constraint sets. Trained extractors, cross-model pipelines, and external provers each target the extraction bottleneck directly, as discussed in \S\ref{sec:discussion}.
